name: Yangshao culture
capital: No capital (village sites such as Banpo)
summary: A Neolithic farming culture along the middle Yellow River in China, known for painted pottery and villages such as Banpo.

location.value: The middle reaches of the Yellow River in China.

terrain.value: The loess plateau of the middle Yellow River, with fertile, easily worked soil.
terrain.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

climate.value: Warmer and wetter than today, during the Holocene climatic optimum.
climate.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

resources.value: Loess soil for millet farming, pigs, dogs and wild plants.
resources.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

disasters.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

population.value: No reliable estimate; villages of a few hundred people, such as Banpo.
population.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

urbanisation.value: Villages surrounded by ditches, with houses around a central plaza (e.g. Banpo, Jiangzhai).
urbanisation.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

disease.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

migration.value: Unknown; farming spread gradually along the river.
migration.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

economicBase.value: Millet farming and pig raising, with hunting and fishing.
economicBase.source: Wikipedia: Yangshao culture (checked 6 Nov 2026); Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

tradeRoutes.value: Local exchange of pottery and stone tools.
tradeRoutes.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible; little difference between graves.
wealth.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

moneyAndTax.value: No money; goods were shared or exchanged.
moneyAndTax.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

inequality.value: Mostly equal villages; some richer graves later.
inequality.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

governmentType.value: No states; village communities probably led by elders or clan heads.
governmentType.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

keyRulers.value: No rulers are known; there was no writing.
keyRulers.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

succession.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

institutions.value: Village communities with shared plazas and cemeteries.
institutions.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

stability.source: Wikipedia: Yangshao culture (checked 6 Nov 2026); Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

eliteConflict.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

armyAndTech.value: Unknown; villages such as Banpo had defensive ditches.
armyAndTech.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

majorWars.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

territoryChange.value: Spread along the middle Yellow River (Henan, Shaanxi and Shanxi).
territoryChange.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

alliancesRivals.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

inventions.value: Advances in agriculture, architecture and pottery-making.
inventions.source: Wikipedia: Yangshao culture (checked 6 Nov 2026); Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

scienceEducation.value: Marks on pottery may be early signs, not writing.
scienceEducation.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

openness.value: Unknown; pottery styles spread across a wide area.
openness.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

religion.value: Burials with goods suggest belief in an afterlife.
religion.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

languageWriting.value: No writing; marks on pottery may be early symbols, but are not writing.
languageWriting.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

artsArchitecture.value: Painted red pottery, such as the human-face fish basin from Banpo.
artsArchitecture.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

socialStructure.value: Families and clans living in villages of round and square houses.
socialStructure.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

sharedIdentity.value: A shared culture along the Yellow River.
sharedIdentity.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

neighbours.value: The Hongshan culture to the north-east and the Dawenkou culture to the east.
neighbours.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

ideasReligions.value: Unknown; burials suggest belief in an afterlife.
ideasReligions.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

colonisation.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

riseSignals.value: Appeared around 5000 BCE as millet farming spread.

peakPeriod.value: The 4th millennium BCE (the Miaodigou phase), when it spread most widely.
peakPeriod.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

declineSignals.value: It gradually changed into the Longshan culture.
declineSignals.source: Liu & Chen, The Archaeology of China (2012)

outcome.value: Followed by the Longshan culture, which had larger towns and more inequality.
